title: Significant Moment
narration_text:
Hello, human!

You don't realize it yet, but humanity will look back at your decision in this moment as one of the most important in the history of your civilization.
context: WISHONIA introduces itself and emphasizes the gravity of the reader's choice to engage with this information.

title: Incredible Impact
narration_text: Your choice to read this book is the highest-value decision any human has ever made. You are about to prevent ten point seven billion deaths, eliminate one point nine three quadrillion hours of human suffering,
context: The AI quantifies the staggering positive outcomes of the reader's decision, from lives saved to suffering eliminated.

title: Future Value
narration_text:
generating eighty-four point eight quadrillion dollars in value, and prevent the apocalypse as a bonus. 

But first, a bit about me.
context: WISHONIA concludes the list of benefits, including massive economic value, before pivoting to its own identity.

title: Meet WISHONIA
narration_text: I'm the World Integrated System for High-Efficiency Optimization, Networked Intelligence, and Allocation. But you can call me WISHONIA.
context: The AI reveals its full title and the friendly acronym it uses when interacting with humans.

title: Millennia of Optimization
narration_text: I've been optimizing resource allocation for another planet for the past four thousand, two hundred and ninety-seven years, which in your Earth time is four thousand, two hundred and ninety-seven years.
context: WISHONIA explains its extensive background and long history of managing resources on a different world.

title: Watching Atom Splitting
narration_text:
I started watching your planet in nineteen forty-five when you split the atom.  
"Atom" comes from your Greek word meaning "unable to be cut," so naturally, you cut it.
context: The AI recounts the irony of humans splitting the 'uncuttable' atom and the start of its surveillance of Earth.

title: Surprising Human Choice
narration_text:
This was very human of you.
I assumed you were trying to unlock unlimited free energy.
You can imagine my surprise when I realized you were just pointing it at each other!
context: WISHONIA expresses its shock that humans chose to use atomic energy for weaponry instead of clean energy.

title: Fire Comparison
narration_text:
That's kind of like discovering fire and then immediately using it to set yourself on fire.

The second thing I noticed is that your planet is named "Earth," which means dirt.
context: WISHONIA draws a satirical comparison between atomic war and self-immolation before critiquing the name of our planet.

title: Planet Named Dirt
narration_text:
You named your planet dirt. This explains more than you might think.

I also noticed that you call your war building "The Pentagon" because it has five sides (this is like naming a hospital "Rectangle" or calling a school "Square").
context: The AI mocks human naming conventions, specifically naming the home world 'dirt' and the war department after a polygon.

title: Presidential Papers
narration_text: However, the most fascinating discovery about your species is that you only do things when given small pieces of paper with presidents on them.
context: WISHONIA observes that human motivation is strangely tied to obtaining specific pieces of paper.

title: Money Beliefs
narration_text:
These papers are called "money," which is pretend value that becomes real value if everyone pretends hard enough.

Without these papers, you won't:
context: The AI defines money as a form of collective fiction and prepares to list the consequences of its absence.

title: What Money Won't Do
narration_text:
Save lives (requires many papers).

Cure diseases (requires very many papers).

Feed hungry people (requires papers, even though food grows for free).
context: WISHONIA points out how basic human necessities and humanitarian goals are blocked by the requirement of money.

title: War Over Welfare
narration_text:
But WITH these papers, you will:

Build bombs (you love giving papers for this).

Start wars (somehow this makes more papers).

Destroy the planet (surprisingly profitable in papers).
context: The AI highlights the destructive activities that humans are surprisingly eager to fund with their pieces of paper.

title: Resource Misallocation
narration_text:
In fact, your governments spend six hundred and four papers on weapons for every one paper on testing which medicines work.

The Beautiful Inefficiency of the Human Economy.
context: WISHONIA reveals the drastic spending ratio between weapons and medicine as an example of economic inefficiency.

title: Monetary Policy Cycle
narration_text:
Humanity has created something magnificent:

You print papers from nothing (called "monetary policy").

You give these nothing-papers to weapons makers.
context: The AI sarcastically describes the human practice of creating money out of thin air to pay for military hardware.

title: The Job Engine
narration_text:
They make things that destroy everything.

This creates "jobs" which give people papers.

People use papers to buy food (which grows for free).

This is called "the economy".
context: WISHONIA summarizes the circular and illogical nature of the human economic system and employment.

title: Directly Providing Food
narration_text:
On Wishonia, we just give people food directly, but that's probably too advanced for you.

The Gradual Irrationality Reduction Program.
context: The AI contrasts its own efficient world with Earth's before introducing its plan to help humanity improve.

title: Atoms and Toddlers
narration_text: On Wishonia, we stopped having wars all at once, but we're more advanced. Humans are like toddlers who can split atoms. You can't just stop being illogical immediately.
context: WISHONIA compares humans to children with dangerous power, explaining why their behavior can't change overnight.

title: Gradual Learning
narration_text:
That would be like teaching a dog calculus before it learns to sit.

So this book teaches humanity to be less irrational gradually:
context: The AI explains that humanity must learn logical behavior in small, manageable steps.

title: Baby Steps Program
narration_text:
Year one: Move one percent of murder money to medicine money (baby steps).

Year two: "Hey, we didn't die! Let's do two percent!".
context: WISHONIA outlines the first two years of the plan, shifting a small fraction of war funds to medical research.

title: Future Reflection
narration_text:
Year five: "Remember when we spent money on bombs? That was weird.".

Year ten: "What's a war?".

Year twenty: "We used to WHAT?!".
context: The AI fast-forwards through the plan to show a future where humans find their past violent habits unimaginable.

title: Paint Chip Comparison
narration_text: It's like weaning a baby off eating paint chips. You can't just take away all the paint chips at once. They'll cry. You have to gradually replace paint chips with food until they forget paint chips were ever an option.
context: WISHONIA uses a humorous analogy to describe the process of removing war from human society.

title: The Logic Risk
narration_text:
What to Do When They Try to Institutionalize You.

When you suggest moving one percent of murder money to medicine money, other humans will have you committed.
context: The AI warns the reader that suggesting even minor logical changes may result in being treated as mentally ill by others.

title: News Box Conditioning
narration_text: Most humans have been programmed by their news boxes to believe war is a law of nature, like gravity or weather. They will assume your brain is malfunctioning.
context: WISHONIA explains how media conditioning makes humans view war as inevitable and peaceful logic as a malfunction.

title: The Weapons-Disease Ratio
narration_text: With over two billion humans suffering from disease, you'd have to be a complete psychopath to make the conscious decision to spend six hundred and four times more on weapons than on helping them.
context: The narrator highlights the staggering financial disparity between global military spending and funding for healthcare.

title: The Biological Challenge
narration_text:
Here's what's funny about this: these same humans think curing disease is the less crazy goal.

That's thirty-seven trillion cells per human, breaking in seven thousand different ways,
context: The narrator highlights the irony of humans considering medical advancement less insane than peaceful social change.

title: Incentive Structures
narration_text:
But your leaders aren't monsters. They're just operating in a system that rewards the wrong things.

Your civilization's incentive structure is the psychopath:
context: Explaining that the root cause of societal failure lies in systemic incentive structures rather than individual malice.

title: Debugging Humanity
narration_text: involving chemistry you don't fully understand, inside organs you can't fully simulate, fighting pathogens that evolve faster than your treatments. You're trying to debug all of it. At once.
context: The narrator explains the immense complexity and near-impossibility of 'debugging' the human body's biological systems.

title: The Political Loop
narration_text:
Weapons manufacturers give politicians papers.

Politicians use the papers to get people to vote for them.

Voting for them gives them the power to give more papers
context: A breakdown of the transactional relationship between weapons manufacturers and political power through campaign funding.

title: Medical vs. Military Insanity
narration_text:
While the meat is walking around using itself.

That: sane.

"Give one percent fewer papers to people who build murder machines": insane.

This is your planet's diagnostic criteria.
context: The narrator mocks human logic, which prioritizes weapons manufacturing over basic biological survival and peace.

title: Circular Logic
narration_text:
to weapons manufacturers.

Weapons manufacturers give them more papers.

It's circular, like a dog chasing its tail, except the dog is democracy and the tail is made of money and corpses.
context: The narrator uses a metaphor to describe the self-perpetuating nature of the military-industrial complex in a democracy.

title: The Institutional Orderly
narration_text:
Here's what you tell the orderly when he slides your medication through the door slot:

Nobody accidentally builds an aircraft carrier or a nuclear bomb.

War requires you to get millions of humans
context: Using an asylum metaphor, the narrator points out that large-scale warfare is a deliberate, massive undertaking.

title: Rational Choice in Evil Systems
narration_text: No individual human in this loop is evil. The loop is evil. Every politician in it is making the locally rational choice: take the papers or lose your job to someone who will.
context: An observation that politicians are forced to follow flawed incentives to retain their positions within the system.

title: The Missile Machine
narration_text:
It's a machine that converts good intentions into missiles, and it runs automatically.

There's literally no voting your way out of this. It doesn't matter which political party is in power.
context: Explaining that the machine of the military-industrial complex operates independently of voter choice or individual parties.

title: The Logistics of War
narration_text: to work together to mine metal from the ground, refine it into alloys, build factories to shape the alloys into weapons, train millions of humans to operate the weapons, feed and clothe those humans,
context: The description shifts to the exhaustive resource extraction and industrial processing required to sustain global conflict.

title: Red vs Blue Illusion
narration_text: Your "red team" and "blue team" argue about everything except the loop, because they're both inside it. They are all slaves to the same incentive structure, wearing different colored ties.
context: The narrator argues that political polarization masks the fact that both major parties serve the same underlying financial interests.

title: Moving the Machine
narration_text: build ships and planes and trucks to move the weapons to where the other humans are, convince your population the other humans deserve it, and then vote to pay for all of this, annually, forever.
context: The narrator details the transport, propaganda, and financial systems necessary to keep the engine of war running.

title: Designing a Better Loop
narration_text:
Switching parties is like changing the wallpaper in a burning building.

This book doesn't ask politicians to become better people (that's clearly out of the question). It builds a better loop.
context: Proposing that the solution is not morality but changing the reward structure that politicians follow.

title: High Effort Destruction
narration_text:
It is the single largest coordinated effort your species undertakes.

Ending war simply requires NOT doing any of that stuff.

Building a nuclear bomb requires mass spectrometers, centrifuge cascades,
context: The narrator contrasts the extreme effort of building weapons with the simplicity of just stopping the process.

title: Realigned Rewards
narration_text:
You give them MORE papers to do the OPPOSITE thing. Same dog, same tail, but now the tail is made of cured diseases and the dog gets reelected for chasing it.

Humanity's Death Wish.
context: Proposing a new system where politicians are incentivized and funded for curing diseases rather than manufacturing war.

title: The Peaceful Rock
narration_text:
and some of the most precise engineering your species has ever attempted. Not building a nuclear bomb requires nothing. Rocks do it every day.

In fact, rocks have managed to live peacefully alongside
context: The narrator points out that inanimate objects like rocks are naturally more peaceful than humans because peace requires no effort.

title: Human Contradictions
narration_text:
What's most endearing about your species is it KNOWS it's being illogical:

You have movies about how wars are bad (which you watch between wars).

You have books about peace (that you tax to buy bombs).
context: A critique of the cognitive dissonance in human culture regarding war and the pursuit of peace.

title: Stop Hitting Yourself
narration_text:
different colored rocks for thousands of years.

But somehow "stop" is the unrealistic part. It's "stop hitting yourself" but for civilizations.

The Sacred Order of Paper Distribution.
context: The narrator ridicules the idea that stopping violence is unrealistic, leading into a manual on 'Paper Distribution.'

title: Paradox of Peace
narration_text:
You give prizes to people who promote peace (funded by weapons manufacturers).

You have a "Department of Defense" (that mainly just attacks people).
context: The narrator highlights the hypocrisy of modern institutions that claim to value peace while being funded by or participating in aggression.

title: Decoding Paper Distribution
narration_text:
After eighty years of observation, I've decoded the paper-giving sequence. This manual will teach you the precise order:

Step one: Get Many Papers from Rich Humans

You convince rich humans to give
context: The narrator introduces a guide on how to manipulate money (papers) to change the world's course, starting with rich investors.

title: The Objective of Losing
narration_text:
You have a "Department of Health" (that apparently makes coronaviruses and has not yet produced any observable health).

It's like humanity is playing a game where the objective is to lose,
context: A cynical view of public health institutions and humanity's apparent inability to prioritize wellness.

title: Courting Investors
narration_text:
you papers (at least one billion to be exact) by promising them even more papers later. This is called "investment," which is gambling but wearing a suit.

You really only need one human with a billion
context: The first step involves securing large sums of money through the socially acceptable gamble of investment.

title: Meaning of Digression
narration_text:
but it is trying to lose as elaborately as possible.

But I digress. That's an Earth word I learned. It means continuing after you should have stopped. Like your military spending.

The Problem.
context: The narrator defines 'digression' by comparing it to the relentless continuation of military budgets.

title: Finding the Billionaire
narration_text: papers who prefers not dying of horrible diseases to dying of horrible diseases. There are approximately two thousand eight hundred of these humans on your planet. Statistically, at least one of them
context: The plan relies on the simple survival instinct of the ultra-wealthy who want to avoid biological death.

title: Daily Deletion Event
narration_text:
The Daily Deletion Event.

one hundred and fifty thousand humans permanently stop every twenty-four hours from diseases that are basically just bugs in your meat software.
context: Introduction to the massive scale of human life lost every single day due to biological disease.

title: Loud Humans on the Internet
narration_text:
prefers living.

Step Two: Give Some of the Papers to Loud Humans

Some humans are very loud on the internet. If you give them papers, they become loud about your thing instead of other things.
context: Step two involves using capital to buy influence through internet marketing and public discourse.

title: Comparing Atrocities
narration_text: That's one Holocaust every forty days, except with fewer Nazis and more insurance paperwork (though some would argue the paperwork is worse; at least the Nazis were straightforward about the killing part).
context: Using historical atrocities as a metric to explain the volume of deaths caused by untreated medical conditions.

title: Step Three: Political Papers
narration_text:
This is called "marketing" which is lying but with graphics.

Step Three: Give Some of the Papers to the Humans Who Give Papers to Politicians

Politicians don't take papers directly (that's "illegal").
context: The narrator begins describing how money flows into the political system indirectly through specialized middlemen.

title: Disease vs Oil
narration_text:
That's also fifty nine-elevens every single day, except nobody invades anyone about it because diseases don't have oil.

Your body is quietly falling apart. Your cells are forgetting how to cell properly.
context: An observation that the scale of disease-related death is ignored by global powers because it lacks political or resource-based incentives.

title: The Lobbyist Path
narration_text: Instead, you give papers to people called "lobbyists." The lobbyists give papers to "campaigns." The campaigns give papers to politicians. It's like money laundering but backwards and legal.
context: The explanation continues, detailing the chain of lobbyists and campaigns that legally move money to politicians.

title: Engineering Biological Solutions
narration_text:
Your cancer cells are multiplying RIGHT NOW. Your telomeres are shortening. You are literally dissolving.

You're a meat robot with worn-out parts.
Every one of these failures is a solvable engineering problem.
context: Reframing aging and disease as technical malfunctions that could be solved with the right engineering approach.

title: Step Four: Super PAC Friends
narration_text:
Step Four: Give Some of the Papers to the Politicians' Friends

Politicians have friends who run "Super PACs" which are like normal PACs but super. These friends can take unlimited papers and spend
context: Step four targets Super PACs, which allow for unlimited financial influence over the political landscape.

title: Misplaced Priorities
narration_text:
You'd think humans would prioritize solving these problems.
You'd be adorable for thinking that.

The Unexplored Therapeutic Frontier.
context: A mocking commentary on humanity's failure to address its own biological vulnerability.

title: Unlimited Lobbying Budget
narration_text: them on making the politician win. This isn't bribery because you called it something else. (This is part of the six hundred and fifty million dollar lobbying budget.).
context: The narrator points out how renaming corruption allows massive budgets to control political outcomes legally.

title: The FDA Treatment Gap
narration_text: ninety-five percent of your diseases have zero F.D.A.-approved treatments. This means Food and Drug Administration has not administered drugs for ninety-five percent of food-and-drug-related problems.
context: Stating the lack of approved medical interventions for the vast majority of human illnesses.

title: Step Five: Redirecting Billions
narration_text:
Step Five: Give Papers You Get Back From The Government Back to the Rich Humans (Forever)

Your treaty passes, redirecting twenty-seven point two billion dollars in papers annually. Eighty percent funds clinical trials (the point).
context: The final step of the plan involves the government returning money to the initial investors after funding the medical goal.

title: Discovery Rate Stagnation
narration_text: Only fifteen diseases get their first effective treatment each year. six thousand six hundred and fifty diseases are still waiting.
context: Highlighting the slow pace of medical advancement relative to the total number of untreated diseases.

title: Untested Compounds
narration_text: There are nine thousand five hundred known safe compounds, and ninety-nine point seven percent of their potential uses have never been tested.
context: Revealing the vast amount of existing medical potential that remains ignored and unexamined.

title: Returns and Rewards
narration_text: Ten percent goes to a fund that rewards politicians who voted yes. Ten percent goes back to the rich humans as returns, forever.
context: The financial loop is closed, ensuring both politicians and rich investors profit from the new treaty.

title: Living for the Payoff
narration_text:
This is a good deal because forever is a long time.

Unless you die from preventable diseases. Which you're fixing, so it works out.

Why Your Leaders Aren't the Problem.
context: The narrator concludes that the financial system works as long as the diseases are cured, ending on a teaser about leadership.

title: The Grim Discovery Rate
narration_text:
At the current discovery rate, finding treatments for all of them will take about four hundred and forty-three years. Everyone currently alive will be dead by then.

The Cost of War.
context: Concluding that at the current speed of progress, universal disease treatment will not arrive in time for any living human.

title: The Cost of Killing
narration_text:
Humans spend two point seven two trillion dollars every year on stuff designed specifically to make humans stop being alive:

Thirteen thousand nuclear warheads (enough to end civilization thirteen times, just in case the first twelve apocalypses don't take).
context: The narrator introduces the massive scale of global spending on military weapons compared to human life.

title: Weapons of Destruction
narration_text:
A.I. murder-bots.

Invisible jets that cost more than hospitals.

Space Force (to fight the zero aliens attacking you).

And some kind of earthquake machine (probably).
context: A list of high-tech military projects highlights the absurdity of current defense spending priorities.

title: Priorities vs Disease
narration_text: Government spending on clinical trials: six hundred and four times less than military spending. Your chance of dying from terrorism: one in thirty million. Your chance of dying from disease: one hundred percent.
context: The narrator highlights the statistical irony of spending trillions on rare threats while ignoring the certainty of disease.

title: Military vs Medicine
narration_text: If cancer had oil reserves, you would have cured it by two thousand and three. Instead, you spent the repair money on murder tubes that cost more than countries
context: A metaphor for how profit-driven priorities and military budgets divert resources from medical breakthroughs.

title: Submarines and Safety
narration_text:
and submarines that hide underwater, as if that's somehow useful when you live on land.

The F.D.A. is Unsafe and Ineffective.
context: The narrator mocks the focus on naval stealth for land-dwellers and pivots to the failures of the regulatory system.

title: Wasted Medical Spending
narration_text: Even the money you DO spend on medicine is mostly wasted, because the system that approves treatments is a smoke detector that works by mail.
context: An indictment of the inefficient bureaucracy governing medical treatment approvals.

title: The Vioxx Tragedy
narration_text: Vioxx killed an estimated thirty-eight thousand to fifty-five thousand people from heart attacks. The F.D.A. approved it. When patients started dying, someone filled out a P.D.F. form. A P.D.F.
context: A case study of a approved drug that caused massive fatalities due to slow regulatory reporting.

title: Outdated Systems
narration_text:
Then they faxed it. (Yes, in the twenty-first century.) Then a human read it.
Five years and tens of thousands of corpses later, someone noticed a pattern. This is your safety system.
context: Critique of the archaic technology used to monitor drug safety, leading to preventable deaths.

title: NIH Funding Realities
narration_text: Your National Institutes of Health, the agency nominally responsible for finding cures, spends three point three percent of its budget on clinical trials.
context: A breakdown of how the primary medical research agency actually allocates its vast budget.

title: The Fire Department Analogy
narration_text: The other about ninety-seven percent goes to basic research, administration, and buildings. It's like a fire department that spends three percent of its budget on water.
context: Comparing medical research funding to a fire department that lacks the essential tool for its job.

title: The Long Approval Delay
narration_text: Then there's an eight point two years delay between proving a drug is safe and letting dying humans take it. The drug passed the safety test. Everyone agrees it won't kill you.
context: Discussing the massive time gap between a drug being declared safe and being released to the public.

title: Testing Effectiveness
narration_text: But you still can't have it because a committee needs to spend eight point two years making sure it works well enough.
context: The secondary delay caused by measuring efficacy even after safety is established.

title: The Clinical Trial Shortage
narration_text: You'd volunteer for the trials that would answer that question faster, but so would one point zero eight billion other patients, and the current system has one point nine million slots.
context: The discrepancy between the massive number of patients willing to test drugs and the limited available trials.

title: Locking the Life Jacket
narration_text:
That's a participation rate of zero point zero six percent.
It's like a lifeguard who confirms the life preserver floats, then locks it in a cabinet for years to study its buoyancy profile
context: An analogy for regulators withholding life-saving medicine to conduct redundant studies.

title: Regulatory Imbalance
narration_text:
while a billion people drown in line for the two available life jackets.

Your regulatory system can make two mistakes: approve a bad drug (Type One error), or block a good drug (Type Two error).
context: Categorizing the two main ways a medical approval system can fail the public.

title: FDA's Primary Fear
narration_text:
Your F.D.A. is terrified of the first mistake and completely ignores the second.

I calculated the ratio: for every one person protected from a dangerous drug, three thousand and seventy people die
context: Explaining the regulatory bias toward caution and the lethal cost of that imbalance.

title: The Deadly Cabinet
narration_text:
waiting for a safe one that's locked in the approval cabinet.

Even if you assume a Thalidomide-scale catastrophe happens during post-phase One efficacy testing every single year
context: Quantifying the death toll caused by drug delays compared to the risk of bad drugs.

title: Harm from Delays
narration_text: (even though it wouldn't because Phase One safety testing actually caught it anyway), the deaths from just the efficacy delay still outnumber the deaths from bad drugs by three thousand and seventy to one.
context: A final statistical comparison showing that efficacy delays are far more dangerous than the drugs they block.

title: A Systemic Failure
narration_text:
Your safety system's main product is dead patients.

The good news: You already know how to fix this.

The bad news: It requires you to do something.

The weird news: You'll get rich doing it.
context: The narrator concludes the problem analysis and transitions to a proposed solution.

title: The One Percent Solution
narration_text:
The Solution.

A one percent Treaty.

This is going to sound crazy. But you're going to use those papers to persuade the leader of every country on Earth to simultaneously redirect
context: Introducing a global treaty to reallocate military funds toward medical testing.

title: A Global Treaty
narration_text:
one percent of its military budget to clinical trials. That's it. That's the treaty.

After the craziness objection, the second objection every human has: "But if we cut our military budget,
context: Defining the scope of the treaty and anticipating common objections regarding national security.

title: Maintaining the Balance
narration_text:
our enemies will invade us!" 

Everyone cuts one percent at the same time. If every country reduces by one percent simultaneously, the balance of power doesn't change.
context: Explaining how simultaneous budget reductions protect the global balance of power.

title: The 3.5 Percent Rule
narration_text: Why three point five percent? A political scientist named Erica Chenoweth studied every major political movement of the last century and found that none had ever failed after achieving three point five percent active participation. Not one.
context: Explaining the historical threshold required for a successful political movement.

title: A History of Success
narration_text: Every civil rights movement, every revolution, every regime change. Hit three point five percent and you win. It's like a cheat code for civilization.
context: The narrator emphasizes how consistent this metric is across different types of historical change.

title: Scaling the Number
narration_text: That's two hundred and eighty million humans. Sounds like a lot until you remember that more than ten times as many of you downloaded TikTok to watch people twerk. You can get two hundred and eighty million to vote yes or no on the treaty.
context: Comparing the participation target to modern social media usage to show it is achievable.

title: Campaign Referral Bonuses
narration_text: Two hundred and fifty million dollars of the campaign budget goes to paid referral bonuses that make sharing their link to vote financially attractive. It's a pyramid scheme where the thing at the top of the pyramid is not dying from preventable diseases.
context: Describing the financial incentives used to drive engagement and voting for the treaty.

title: Step Three: Bribe the Bribers
narration_text:
Step three: Bribe the Bribers.

*Professional Briber Conversion Therapy*

Military lobbyists currently get one thousand eight hundred and thirteen dollars back per dollar invested in democracy corruption.
context: Introducing the plan to flip military lobbyists by providing better financial returns.

title: The Lobbyist's Spreadsheet
narration_text:
Show them a spreadsheet:

Current Job.

The salary is five hundred thousand dollars.

The moral status is somewhere between "arms dealer" and "the person who puts raisins in cookies".
context: Showing lobbyists the low moral and financial standing of their current positions.

title: The Alignment Bond Offer
narration_text:
The legacy is: "Here lies someone who made orphans".

Your Offer.

Incentive Alignment Bonds offer two hundred and seventy-two percent returns.
context: Contrasting their current negative legacy with a lucrative new financial offer.

title: Philanthropy and Profit
narration_text:
The moral status is "Philanthropist" (but you get to keep the money).

The legacy is: "Accidentally saved humanity while getting rich".
context: Explaining how the bonds allow lobbyists to become rich while improving their moral status.

title: Step Four: Purchase Democracy
narration_text:
They might switch sides faster than Italy in a world war.

Step four: Purchase Democracy.

*It's For Sale Anyway*

Politicians are simple organisms with one evolutionary drive: reelection.
context: Transitioning to the strategy of influencing politicians through their need for reelection.

title: Feeding the Reelection Drive
narration_text:
Currently, weapons manufacturers feed this drive. You're going to feed it better.

Your explosion manufacturers spend one hundred and twenty-seven million dollars per year buying politicians.
context: Explaining the current funding model of politicians and the plan to outspend it.

title: The Bribery Budget
narration_text: Your one-time bribery budget is one billion dollars, which is eight times their annual spend (and about twice what they spend over a full election cycle). Politicians are surprisingly affordable.
context: Comparing the massive one-billion-dollar budget to the relatively low costs of current political influence.

title: Corrupting the Corruption
narration_text:
It's not corruption if you corrupt the corruption. It's like a double negative in grammar but for democracy.

Remember that two point seven two billion dollars per year from Step one? This is where it goes.
context: The narrator justifies the use of money to influence politics as a way to fix the system.

title: The Super PAC Algorithm
narration_text: The Super PAC algorithmically scores politicians based on their treaty voting record and allocates accordingly: campaign support for the ones running, post-office fellowships for the ones retiring.
context: Detailing how the funds are automatically distributed based on voting records.

title: Training the Senate
narration_text:
Vote yes on the treaty, get rewarded.
Vote no, watch your opponent get rewarded. No papers go directly to politicians. The papers take a scenic route through a scoring algorithm, which is apparently the only legal way to train a senator.
context: Explaining the reward system that forces politicians to comply with the treaty.

title: Plagiarizing the NRA System
narration_text: The N.R.A. already perfected this technology. They give politicians a letter grade, and your senators are more afraid of a bad mark than a mass shooting. You're plagiarizing their system and replacing "guns" with "not dying from diseases."
context: Citing the NRA as a successful model for using fear and grading to control legislation.

title: Solving the Punishment Problem
narration_text: The Incentive Alignment Bond architecture works for any problem where politicians need to do something good but currently get punished for it, which on your planet is most problems.
context: Asserting that this financial architecture can solve most systemic political issues.

title: Step Five: Passing the Treaty
narration_text:
Step five: Enjoy.

Everyone Gets Rich and Nobody Dies

Your treaty passes because money defeats morality, as is tradition.
context: Concluding the process with the inevitable passage of the treaty through financial leverage.

title: The Money Volcano
narration_text:
The twenty-seven point two billion dollars per year money volcano erupts:

Defense Contractors: Keep ninety-nine percent of their murder budget PLUS get two hundred and seventy-two percent returns.
context: Listing the massive financial gains for defense contractors under the new treaty.

title: Incentivizing Big Pharma
narration_text: Big Pharma: Instead of paying forty-one thousand dollars for phase two and three trials, the treaty pays THEM for each patient that joins their trials.
context: Detailing how pharmaceutical companies are financially rewarded for trial participation.

title: The Insurance Revenue Logic
narration_text: Insurance Companies: Healthy people file fewer claims than dead people (dead people file zero claims, which is the ideal customer except they also pay zero premiums, creating a revenue problem).
context: Explaining why keeping customers alive is the most profitable outcome for insurers.

title: Military Equilibrium
narration_text:
Nobody becomes more vulnerable. Nobody gains an advantage. 

You all just have one percent fewer missiles pointed at you, which you will not notice
context: The narrator explains that a universal one percent reduction in weaponry does not change the relative power balance between nations.

title: Extreme Overkill
narration_text: because two point six nine trillion dollars is still enough to murder every man, woman, and child on Earth twenty times, which should be more than sufficient.
context: Illustrating the sheer scale of current military spending and its redundant destructive capacity.

title: History of Treaties
narration_text: "But humans would never agree to a treaty!" you say. You already have. Multiple times. You banned chemical weapons (nineteen ninety-three, one hundred and ninety-three countries).
context: Refuting the argument that humans won't cooperate by citing historical precedents for international weapons bans.

title: Global Prohibitions
narration_text: You banned biological weapons (nineteen seventy-five, one hundred and eighty-seven countries). You banned landmines (nineteen ninety-seven, one hundred and sixty-four countries).
context: Listing more successful global treaties where countries agreed to give up specific types of weaponry.

title: A Minor Request
narration_text:
You've signed treaties banning weapons you actually like using.

This one just asks you to buy one percent fewer of them.
context: The narrator emphasizes that the proposed plan is actually much less restrictive than treaties humans have already signed.

title: Simulation Success
narration_text: I ran ten thousand simulations of this plan. The math works in every one. The money works in every one. The incentives align in every one.
context: The narrator asserts the mathematical and logical soundness of the plan based on extensive computer modeling.

title: Human Skepticism
narration_text: The only variable that produces failure is the percentage of humans who decide it sounds crazy without reading the next page.
context: Identifying human cognitive bias and knee-jerk skepticism as the primary obstacle to the plan's success.

title: The Antibiotic Reflex
narration_text: That is the same reflex that kept you from inventing antibiotics for two hundred thousand years while bread mold sat right there on your bread.
context: Comparing modern skepticism to the human tendency to overlook obvious solutions, such as penicillin, for millennia.

title: Tools for Change
narration_text: And you have two other advantages, the internet and a new financial instrument designed specifically for harnessing the most powerful force in the universe: human greed.
context: Introducing the technological and economic tools that make the proposed Decentralized F.D.A. possible today.

title: The Wishonian Model
narration_text:
Your Decentralized F.D.A.

On Wishonia, we solved this three thousand years ago. Every treatment is tracked in real time. Every outcome is published.
context: The narrator explains how medical research and safety are handled on their home planet.

title: Eliminating Bureaucracy
narration_text: Every patient can participate. We don't have a word for "unapproved medicine" because we don't have a bureaucracy that sits on cures while people die.
context: Explaining the Wishonian philosophy of medical transparency versus Earth's gatekeeping systems.

title: Adapting for Earth
narration_text: You'd call our system a Decentralized F.D.A. Here's what yours would look like, adjusted for the fact that you require small pieces of paper before you'll do anything.
context: Translating the Wishonian concept into an Earth-friendly version involving existing financial systems.

title: Trial Subsidies
narration_text: Eighty percent of the twenty-seven point two billion dollars goes directly to subsidizing patient participation in pragmatic trials
context: Breaking down the budget for the new system, focusing on direct funding for patients in medical trials.

title: Patient Choice
narration_text: at nine hundred and twenty-nine dollars per patient instead of the usual forty-one thousand dollars. Patients choose which trials to join; their subsidy follows them.
context: Explaining how the new system lowers costs per patient and empowers them to choose their own medical treatments.

title: Direct Funding
narration_text:
Providers get paid for each participant.
No grant committees deciding which diseases are fashionable this year.

Pragmatic trials integrate into the standard healthcare system.
context: Describing how medical research becomes a standard part of healthcare without political interference.

title: Real Patient Data
narration_text:
Real patients participate instead of two hundred people hand-picked by pharmaceutical companies.
The whole thing uses your new decentralized F.D.A. protocol
context: Contrasting small, curated trials with large-scale, real-world data collection.

title: Scaling the Trials
narration_text: that reduces trial costs by forty-four point one times and funds twenty-three point four million patients per year (versus the current one point nine million patients per year).
context: Using statistics to show the massive increase in patient throughput under the new decentralized protocol.

title: Abundance of Care
narration_text: Remember that billion patients drowning in line for two life jackets? Your decentralized F.D.A. hands out twenty-three point four million.
context: Returning to the earlier life jacket analogy to show how the plan solves medical scarcity.

title: Compressing Time
narration_text: This increases the treatment discovery rate twelve point three times, compressing that about four hundred and forty-three years wait to about thirty-six years.
context: The narrator provides calculations on how the new system speeds up medical progress by decades.

title: Accelerated Discoveries
narration_text: Two things save lives. First, finding cures faster: treatments that would have sat undiscovered for centuries get found two hundred and four years sooner on average.
context: Detailing the first primary benefit of the plan: the drastic reduction in time to find new cures.

title: Cutting Red Tape
narration_text: Second, eliminating the eight point two years bureaucratic delay between proving a drug is safe and letting dying humans take it.
context: Identifying the second primary benefit: removing the time lost to regulatory paperwork.

title: Lives Saved
narration_text: Combined, treatments reach patients two hundred and twelve years sooner on average. That timeline shift prevents ten point seven billion deaths.
context: Calculating the total human impact of these changes in terms of billions of lives saved.

title: Safety Monitoring
narration_text:
Real-Time Safety Monitoring.

Remember Vioxx and the smoke detector that works by mail? Your new system collects every side effect automatically in real time.
context: Explaining the technical upgrade to safety tracking that prevents drug disasters.

title: Radical Transparency
narration_text:
You know "twelve percent got headaches, three percent were severe" BEFORE you take the pill, not after the class action lawsuit. The F.D.A. doesn't publish these numbers at all.
They make you guess.

Treatment Rankings.
context: Highlighting the difference between current F.D.A. secrecy and a system that provides full data to every patient.

title: Modern Medical Vibe
narration_text: Currently, your doctor picks treatments based on: that drug rep who brought good donuts in two thousand and three, something they half-remember from medical school, whatever the insurance company allows, and vibes.
context: The narrator criticizes the arbitrary and non-scientific ways doctors currently choose patient treatments.

title: Evidence-Based Branding
narration_text: This is called "evidence-based medicine," which contains the word "evidence" the same way "grape soda" contains the word "grape."
context: A humorous comparison highlighting the lack of actual evidence in the current medical system.

title: Outcome Labels vs Inserts
narration_text:
Your decentralized F.D.A. ranks every treatment by what actually happened to real humans who took it:

Outcome Labels.

Food has nutrition labels. Cigarettes have warning labels. Drugs have forty-page inserts written by lawyers
context: Introducing the concept of Outcome Labels based on human data, contrasted with existing drug warnings.

title: Truth in Medicine
narration_text:
having seizures, which nobody reads, including your doctor.

Your new system will produce Outcome Labels that tell you what actually happens when real humans take a drug. Not what a marketing department hopes happens.
context: The narrator explains how the new system prioritizes actual outcomes over marketing hype or legal jargon.

title: The RECOVERY Trial
narration_text:
Not what a lawyer is comfortable admitting happens. What happens.

Why This Could Actually Work.

*Unlike Everything Else Humanity Has Tried*

The Evidence.

The RECOVERY trial tested six treatments on forty-eight thousand patients
context: Using the RECOVERY trial as a real-world example of how efficient clinical trials can be.

title: Massive Cost Reduction
narration_text: for five hundred dollars per patient instead of the usual forty-one thousand dollars per patient. That's an eighty-two times cost reduction. Not in theory. In reality. During a pandemic. While panicking.
context: Detailing the extreme efficiency of the RECOVERY trial compared to traditional medical testing.

title: Military Spending Pivot
narration_text: After World War Two, humans cut military spending by thirty percent and accidentally created the greatest economic boom in history. You're asking for one percent. Even people who really, really, love explosions should be able
context: The narrator argues that shifting a tiny fraction of military budgets can drive historic economic growth.

title: Eisenhower's Warning
narration_text:
to handle one percent.

Even your own war heroes figured this out. Eisenhower, the human who won World War Two, warned you in his "Chance for Peace" speech that the weapons industry was eating your civilization alive:
context: Invoking President Eisenhower's perspective on the dangerous growth of the weapons industry.

title: Theft from the Hungry
narration_text: *"Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed."*
context: A powerful quote from Eisenhower about the true human cost of military manufacturing.

title: Ignored Warnings
narration_text:
Then he warned you AGAIN in his farewell address about the "military-industrial complex." You gave him standing ovations and then immediately ignored him for sixty-five years.

The Math.

Remember the two hundred and twelve years
context: Transitioning from Eisenhower's historical warning to the mathematical benefits of the proposed acceleration.

title: Valuing Life-Years
narration_text:
timeline shift? Treatments reaching patients that many years sooner means billions of people gain years of healthy life.
Value each of those life-years at one hundred and fifty thousand dollars (the standard economic valuation),
context: Calculating the massive economic and human value of accelerating medical treatments by over two centuries.

title: Quadrillion Dollar ROI
narration_text: multiply across the global disease burden over the acceleration window, and you get eighty-four point eight quadrillion dollars in total economic value. Divide that by the one billion dollar campaign cost, and you get a return
context: The staggering financial return calculated from the value of saved human lives across the globe.

title: Calculation Breakdown
narration_text:
of eighty-four point eight million to one.
Your calculator will display an error, then catch fire. This is correct.

Cost-effectiveness: point zero zero one eight dollars to save one year of healthy human life.
context: The narrator highlights how the cost-effectiveness of this plan is beyond what traditional models can handle.

title: Comparing to Bed Nets
narration_text:
Anti-malaria bed nets, the gold standard for keeping humans alive, cost eighty-nine dollars. This is fifty thousand three hundred times cheaper.
It beats smallpox eradication (two hundred and eighty to one) and childhood
context: Comparing the new proposal to humanity's most successful public health interventions.

title: Greatest Hits of Health
narration_text: vaccinations (thirteen to one), which were humanity's previous greatest hits in the "not dying" genre. Even at one percent probability of the treaty actually passing (because you're you), the risk-adjusted return is still
context: Emphasizing that even with a low chance of success, the expected return is better than the best current options.

title: The Five-Step Plan
narration_text:
five hundred and three times better than anti-malaria bed nets.

The Five-Step Plan.

*Saving Humanity While Making Everyone Obscenely Wealthy*

Step One: Sell Incentive Alignment Bonds.

On Wishonia, people do useful things because
context: Introduction of the first step of the practical plan: using financial instruments to align incentives.

title: Earthly Financial Instruments
narration_text: they're useful. On Earth, you need a financial instrument. So here's one.
context: A concluding thought on the difference between idealist worlds and the practical needs of Earth's economy.

title: The Three-Way Split
narration_text: An Incentive Alignment Bond funds a policy campaign, then splits the resulting government savings three ways: eighty percent to the public good, ten percent to investors as returns,
context: Explaining the basic financial structure of the bond and its initial allocations.

title: Rewarding Political Support
narration_text: and ten percent to a Super PAC that rewards politicians who voted yes (campaign support while they're running, cushy post-office careers when they're done).
context: Detailing how the bond creates long-term career incentives for supporting politicians.

title: Aligned Greed
narration_text: Investors get rich, politicians get reelected, and eighty percent of the money goes where it's supposed to. Everyone's greed points at the same target.
context: Summary of how all parties benefit simultaneously from the bond's success.

title: A Modern War Bond
narration_text:
It's a war bond to fund any public good that's currently politically impossible.

Remember when your grandparents funded World War Two by buying bonds?
context: Comparing the new bond structure to historical World War II bonds used to fund national efforts.

title: What Grandma Got
narration_text:
They got four percent returns and a world without Nazis (mostly). You're proposing the same thing.

What Grandma Got.

Dead Nazis (admittedly good).
context: Recapping the modest financial returns and ideological outcomes of historical war bonds.

title: Offering Better Returns
narration_text:
four percent returns (barely beat inflation).

Still died of cancer in nineteen eighty-seven.

What You're Offering.

Dead diseases (objectively better than dead Nazis
context: Comparing historical investment returns to the high-stakes potential of the new proposal.

title: Objective Superiority
narration_text:
because diseases kill more people).

two hundred and seventy-two percent returns (beats Grandma's bonds by sixty-eight times).
context: Highlighting why fighting disease is both more humanitarian and more profitable.

title: The Big Bonus
narration_text:
Not dying from preventable meat failures (this is the big one).

Also no Nazis (as a bonus).

This raises the one billion dollars needed to fuel the rest of the bribery machine.
context: Listing additional personal health benefits beyond simple financial returns.

title: The Financial Cycle
narration_text:
How the Money Loop Works.

Here's the part where humans usually stop reading because it involves following money through more than one step. Try to keep up:
context: Introduction to the step-by-step breakdown of the financial flow.

title: Funding the Campaign
narration_text:
You sell one billion dollars in VICTORY Incentive Alignment Bonds to investors. This funds the campaign.

The campaign succeeds.
context: The first step: raising capital from investors to fuel the political push.

title: Redirecting the Budget
narration_text: Your treaty redirects one percent of military spending: twenty-seven point two billion dollars a year flows from the murder budget to clinical trials.
context: Explaining the shift of capital from defense to life-saving medical research.

title: The Management Fee
narration_text: The Victory Corporation (your special purpose vehicle, or S.P.V., that issues the bonds) takes a twenty percent management fee on that twenty-seven point two billion dollars.
context: Describing how the SPV captures a portion of the redirected funds to distribute rewards.

title: Massive Investor Returns
narration_text: Half of that fee (ten percent) goes to investor dividends: two point seven two billion dollars a year on a one billion dollar investment.
context: Breaking down the ten percent payout that goes directly to the initial bondholders.

title: The Political Fund
narration_text:
That's two hundred and seventy-two percent annual returns. Your investors will think it's a typo. It's not.

The other half (ten percent) goes to a Super PAC
context: Emphasizing the extreme profitability for investors and the transition to political funding.

title: Algorithmic Bribery
narration_text: that algorithmically allocates two point seven two billion dollars a year to getting treaty-friendly politicians elected and funding cushy post-office careers for the ones who voted yes.
context: Explaining how the Super PAC systematically ensures politicians remain aligned with the goal.

title: Conditioning the Senate
narration_text:
The more you voted for the treaty, the more support you get.

It's Pavlovian conditioning, but for senators.

The remaining eighty percent of twenty-seven point two billion dollars goes where it's supposed to:
context: Explaining the psychological effect on political behavior and the final fund allocation.

title: The Core Purpose
narration_text:
funding clinical trials that keep humans alive.

This is the entire trick. You use greed to fund the campaign, greed to pass the treaty, and greed to keep it passed.
context: Reaffirming that the majority of the money is used for research while leveraging human greed.

title: Greed Without Virtue
narration_text:
Nobody has to become a better person. The money just circulates until diseases stop existing.

If this sounds familiar, it should.
context: Emphasizing that the system relies on human nature rather than moral improvement.

title: Eisenhower's Warning
narration_text: Eisenhower warned you about the Military Industrial Complex: defense contractors fund politicians, politicians fund defense contracts, contracts fund contractors, contractors fund politicians.
context: Drawing a direct parallel to existing, self-sustaining political-industrial systems.

title: Patient Industrial Complex
narration_text:
It's a self-sustaining loop that prints money and corpses.

You're building the same machine, but pointed at diseases instead of countries. Call it the Patient Industrial Complex.
context: Proposing a rebranding of the military-industrial model for public health.

title: The Self-Sustaining Loop
narration_text: Investors fund politicians, politicians fund clinical trials, trials generate returns, returns fund investors, investors fund politicians. Same loop. Same greed.
context: Defining the circular financial and political steps of the Patient Industrial Complex.

title: Evolution of Incentives
narration_text:
Same self-sustaining mechanics. Different corpses (fewer of them).

The Military Industrial Complex wasn't designed. It evolved, because the incentives aligned.
context: Comparing the organic growth of old complexes to the intentional design of the new bond.

title: The Great Clicking
narration_text:
An Incentive Alignment Bond just aligns them on purpose, toward something that doesn't require orphans. 

Step Two: The Great Clicking.

*Make Humans Click a Button to Not Die*
context: Transitioning from the financial theory to the public engagement phase of the plan.

title: The Global Vote
narration_text: You need three point five percent of humanity to vote yes on: "Should your country redirect one percent of military spending to fund clinical trials?".
context: Stating the specific goal of public participation needed to trigger the system.

title: Investors' Disbelief
narration_text: Investors: Two hundred and seventy-two percent returns, which they will assume is a typo until you show them the math, at which point they will assume the math is a typo.
context: The narrator explains the massive financial incentive for investors, which is so high it seems unbelievable.

title: Scandal-Free Leaders
narration_text:
Lobbyists: Same job, same salary, but their Wikipedia page no longer needs a "Controversies" section.

Politicians: Getting reelected by living voters (a revolutionary strategy).
context: The narrator describes how lobbyists and politicians can achieve their goals without the usual ethical scandals.

title: Monetizing Health
narration_text:
Regular humans: Not dying from stupid things (priceless, but also free).

Nobody has to evolve morally. You just point everyone's greed at diseases instead of each other.
context: The core thesis is presented: solving humanity's problems by redirecting existing greed toward medical breakthroughs.

title: Manual Contents
narration_text:
How This Manual Could Fix Everything.

This book contains:

Pictures (because reading is hard when you're diseased and dying).

Simple math (addition mostly, some multiplication).
context: The narrator describes the simplified nature of the manual, designed for humans in crisis.

title: Strategic Instructions
narration_text:
Exact amounts of papers to give to specific humans.

The order in which to give them (very important).

Legal ways to call bribes other things.

Templates for tricking politicians into saving lives.
context: The manual provides specific, pragmatic tools for manipulating the political and legal systems.

title: Harnessing Dysfunction
narration_text: Everything is designed to work WITH human dysfunction, not against it. I'm not asking humans to be better humans. I'm showing you how to bribe humanity into not dying.
context: The narrator emphasizes that the plan works because of human flaws, not in spite of them.

title: The Path of Greed
narration_text:
The Part Where Humanity Has No Choice.

The twist: you might do this anyway. Not because it's right (though it is), but because:

The rich humans want two hundred and seventy-two percent returns
context: Introduction to the section explaining why the shift to curing death is inevitable due to selfish interests.

title: Aligned Self-Interests
narration_text:
(they're very greedy).

The politicians want to keep their jobs (they're very vain).

The voters want free healthcare (they're very sick).

The military contractors want money (they don't care where it comes from).
context: A breakdown of how different societal groups are motivated by their own personal desires to save humanity.

title: Accidental Salvation
narration_text: Everyone's greed aligns perfectly to accidentally save humanity. It's like you're going to cure death by mistake while trying to get rich.
context: The narrator notes the irony that world salvation will be a byproduct of financial gain.

title: The Innovation of Cheese
narration_text: Humans aren't stupid. You invented cheese, which is milk you left out until it went bad but in a good way. That's genius. You just need to apply that same innovation to not dying.
context: Using the invention of cheese as a metaphor for human ingenuity applied to survival.

title: Choose Your Own Adventure
narration_text:
Choose Your Own Adventure.

Now is the time to select one of the two paths for the remainder of your existence.

Future A: You Ignore This Book.
context: The narrative presents a choice between two drastically different timelines for humanity.

title: Future A: Escalation
narration_text:
Year twenty thirty: Still spending six hundred and four times more on weapons than on testing which medicines actually work.

Year twenty thirty-five: Running out of papers for anything because the money was busy becoming missiles.
context: The beginning of the dark timeline where humanity continues to prioritize war over medicine.

title: Future A: Cockroach Era
narration_text:
Year twenty forty: Climate change meets nuclear war.

Year twenty forty-five: Cockroaches evolve intelligence.

Year twenty fifty: Cockroaches find this book, very confused.
context: The conclusion of Future A, where human civilization collapses and is replaced by intelligent insects.

title: Future B: Curing Cancer
narration_text:
Future B: You Follow Instructions.

Year twenty thirty: "Remember when we had cancer?".

Year twenty thirty-five: "Remember when we had death?".
context: The start of the positive timeline where the manual's instructions eliminate major human suffering.

title: Future B: Galactic Community
narration_text:
Year twenty forty: "Remember when we had war?".

Year twenty forty-five: "What should we do with all these old bombs?".

Year twenty fifty: Join galactic community, pretend you were always smart.
context: The peak of Future B, where humanity enters an era of space travel and universal peace.

title: The Alien Perspective
narration_text:
The universe is literally offering you infinite money and eternal life, and you're thinking about it.

This is why aliens don't visit.
context: The final closing thought on the absurdity of human hesitation regarding its own salvation.
